{{Distinguish|Geometric continuity|Continuous geometry}}
{{one source|date=April 2024}}
The concept of '''geometrical continuity'''  was primarily applied to the [[conic sections]] (and related shapes) by mathematicians such as [[Gottfried Leibniz|Leibniz]], [[Johannes Kepler|Kepler]], and [[Jean-Victor Poncelet|Poncelet]]. The concept was an early attempt at describing, through geometry rather than algebra, the concept of [[continuous function|continuity]] as expressed through a parametric function.<ref name="Taylor 1911, pp. 674–675">{{cite EB1911|last=Taylor |first=Charles |author-link=Charles Taylor (Hebraist) |wstitle=Geometrical Continuity |volume=11 |pages=674–675}}</ref>

The basic idea behind geometrical continuity was that the five conic sections were really five different versions of the same shape. An [[ellipse]] tends to a [[circle]] as the [[eccentricity (mathematics)|eccentricity]] approaches zero, or to a [[parabola]] as it approaches one; and a [[hyperbola]] tends to a [[parabola]] as the eccentricity drops toward one; it can also tend to intersecting [[line (geometry)|line]]s. Thus, there was ''continuity'' between the conic sections. These ideas led to other concepts of continuity. For instance, if a circle and a straight line were two expressions of the same shape, perhaps a line could be thought of as a circle of infinite [[radius]]. For such to be the case, one would have to make the line closed by allowing the point <math>x =\infty</math> to be a point on the circle, and for <math>x =+\infty</math> and <math>x =-\infty</math> to be identical. Such ideas were useful in crafting the modern, algebraically defined, idea of the [[continuous function|continuity]] of a function and of <math>\infty</math> (see [[projectively extended real line]] for more).<ref name="Taylor 1911, pp. 674–675"/><!-- 1911 covers some of this but needs a modern reference-->
